transcript.content: Hello, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

Thanks, Doctor. Um… I guess what finally pushed me to come in is that I’m having a harder time keeping all the moving parts organized. I’m a software developer, so I’m used to juggling things, but lately it’s like… patent notes, workshop prep, gallery deadlines, team decisions—everything is competing in my head.

I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is, because I do get things done, but I keep finding myself starting whatever feels loudest or most urgent in the moment instead of what actually matters most. And that’s starting to catch up with me, I think.
Would you say you've struggled with this kind of disorganization and distractibility since childhood or adolescence, or is this a new change from how you used to function?

Yeah… I think it’s not totally new. I mean, I did fine in school overall, so I never thought of it as a big issue, but looking back, it was probably there pretty early.

I remember teachers in grade school saying things like I was bright, but I daydreamed a lot. And there were these comments about me forgetting to turn in assignments—even ones I’d actually finished—or losing homework folders. So… I guess it was around before adolescence, if that’s the kind of thing you mean.

Aside from the trouble organizing tasks, do you find yourself frequently worrying excessively about a number of different things—like health, finances, or how things will turn out—even when there's no clear reason to worry?

Um… I don’t think so, not in a constant way. I mean, I worry about normal things—work going okay, deadlines, whether I’m letting people down—but I wouldn’t say I’m sitting around worrying about health or finances or everything that could go wrong for no reason.

At least, I don’t think that’s the main issue. Does that answer what you mean?
Do you often feel restless, fidgety, or find it hard to sit still, or notice yourself acting impulsively—like interrupting others or making quick decisions without thinking them through?

A little, yeah. I wouldn’t say I’m, you know, bouncing off the walls or anything. But on long design calls, I can feel this kind of pressure building in my body, like I need to get up.

So I’ll pace around my office, or shift from one chair to another, even while I’m trying to look like I’m focused and following along. I’m not sure if that’s the kind of restlessness you mean.
Do you often find yourself interrupting people mid-conversation, blurting out responses before they've finished speaking, or making decisions on the spot without really thinking them through?

I don’t think that’s a big pattern for me, no. I mean, I might jump in sometimes if I’m excited or if I think I know where someone is going, but I try pretty hard not to interrupt.

And with decisions… I usually overthink them more than make them too fast, I’d say. So I don’t know that I’d call myself impulsive in that way. Is that the kind of thing you’re asking?

Would you say these organization and focus difficulties are causing real problems in more than one area of your life—like at work, at home, or in your relationships—not just occasionally, but on a regular basis?

Yeah… I think so. I’d like to say it’s just occasional, but it has been showing up in real ways.

At work especially, it’s started to affect how people see me, I think. I missed a checkpoint for a patent filing, which was… embarrassing. And there was this architecture review that didn’t go very well, and afterward I got the sense that some collaborators were questioning whether I can really lead the larger project.

I don’t want to overstate it, but it’s not just me feeling disorganized privately anymore. It’s starting to have consequences. Is that the kind of “real problems” you mean?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports chronic inattentive symptoms (daydreaming, forgetting completed assignments, losing materials) dating back to childhood, with current difficulties in prioritizing/organizing tasks, distractibility, and mild hyperactive restlessness (pacing during calls). These symptoms cause functional impairment across work domains (missed patent filing checkpoint, poor architecture review, colleagues questioning leadership capability). Excessive worry characteristic of GAD was explicitly denied, and impulsivity (interrupting, hasty decisions) was minimal, making ADHD—predominantly inattentive with some hyperactive traits—the best fit over anxiety or unspecified attention disorder.
